title: The Lucena position
summary: Reach the Lucena position and build the bridge that lets the pawn queen against the rook.
part.ponte.title: Building the bridge
part.ponte.summary: In the Lucena position, the rook goes to the fourth rank, the king steps out in front of the pawn, and the rook blocks the last check: the pawn promotes.
part.corte.title: Cutting off the king
part.corte.summary: With the black king glued to the queening square, a check on its file pushes it aside; only then comes the bridge.
part.lateral.title: Side checks
part.lateral.summary: Against the rook checking from far away, from the side, the king walks up to it and attacks it from the pawn's rank, without leaving the pawn.
part.convert.title: From start to finish
part.convert.summary: The whole game: cut off the king, escort the pawn to the Lucena position and promote within the move limit.
ex.ponteAssessment01: Play White and win. The black rook, on g2, checks your king, and the black king is far from the pawn, on c6.
ex.ponteAssessment01.hint: How can the rook, with the king's help, put an end to the checks?
ex.ponteAssessment01.solution: 1.Rg4 blocks the check with the rook protected by the king: that is the bridge. If 1...Rxg4, 2.Kxg4, and the pawn promotes. 1.Kf5 also wins, with the same idea: after the check on f2, the rook blocks on f4.
key.lucena: The Lucena position as Alessandro Salvio published it in 1634: the pawn is one step from promoting and the white king stands in front of it. White wins whoever moves: all that is left is to build the bridge.
history: The Lucena position is the most important one in rook endings: with rook and pawn against rook it is the position that wins, and almost every ending of this kind revolves around reaching it or preventing it. The name is a historical mistake: the Spaniard Luis Ramírez de Lucena wrote one of the first printed chess books around 1497, but the position is not in it; it first appears in 1634, in a book by the Italian Alessandro Salvio. The idea of "building a bridge" with the rook, which is the heart of this lesson, got its name from Aron {{Nimzowitsch|aron-nimzowitsch}} in 1925. Grandmasters know it so well that they rarely need to play it out: in 1999, in Sweden, {{Ulf Andersson|ulf-andersson}} exchanged pawns just to reach it, and his opponent resigned before the bridge ever appeared on the board.
practice: The Lucena position with White to move.
ex.corteAssessment01: Play as White and find the best move. The pawn is on f7, with your king on f8 and the rook on b1; the black king is on d7, and the black rook on g3. Your king has no move.
ex.corteAssessment01.hint: Where would your king step out, and who watches those squares?
ex.corteAssessment01.solution: 1.Rd1+: the check drives the black king from d7, from where it watched your king's way out. If 1...Kc7, the rook stands between it and the pawn, and your king steps out along the e-file; if 1...Ke6, it lets go of e8, and 2.Ke8 takes your king out from in front of the pawn. Other rook moves also win, but the black king keeps watching your king's way out.
part.chegar.title: Escorting the pawn
part.chegar.summary: With the rook cutting off the black king, your king climbs right next to the pawn, sheltered from the checks, until the Lucena position.
ex.chegarAssessment01: Play as White and find the best move. The black rook on h4 checks your king on f4. The pawn is on f5, and the black king on d6 is cut off by your rook on the e-file.
ex.chegarAssessment01.hint: What is the danger of the king moving away from the pawn?
ex.chegarAssessment01.solution: 1.Kg5: the king gets out of check and stays next to the pawn, which remains protected, and it also attacks the rook on h4. Retreating the king to e3, f3 or g3 takes it away from the pawn, and the position is already a draw.
ex.convertAssessment01: Play as White and find the best move. The pawn is on c5, with your king on b4 and the rook on a1; the black king is on e6, and the black rook on h2.
ex.convertAssessment01.hint: Before taking the pawn forward, where does the black king have to be stopped?
ex.convertAssessment01.solution: 1.Rd1: the rook on the d-file cuts off the black king, which can no longer reach the square in front of the pawn; only then do the king and the pawn advance together. After 1.Kb5? Kd7 or 1.Ra6+? Kd7, the black king reaches c7, in front of the pawn, and it is a draw; after 1.c6? Rc2, the black rook attacks the pawn from behind, and it is a draw.
ex.lateralAssessment01: Play as White and find the best move. The black rook on c6 checks your king on e6. The pawn is on f7, and the black king on h7 is cut off by your rook on g4.
ex.lateralAssessment01.hint: Along which rank should the king approach the black rook?
ex.lateralAssessment01.solution: 1.Kd7: the king attacks the rook along the pawn's rank, without leaving the pawn. After 1...Rf6, 2.Ke7 attacks the rook and protects the pawn again, and it promotes. After 1.Ke7? Rc7+, the checks start again, and the king cannot escape them without leaving the pawn: a draw. After 1.Kd5? Rf6, the rook stands behind the pawn and captures it: a draw.
